text: Max-Cut is the 'hello world' of quantum optimization -- nearly every QAOA paper and tutorial benchmarks against it first. Here you'll derive its QUBO formulation from scratch and hand-verify it on a graph small enough to check by eye.

Max-Cut asks you to split a graph's nodes into two groups so the number of edges crossing between them is as large as possible. For a single edge between nodes i and j, the expression x_i plus x_j minus 2 x_i x_j equals 1 exactly when the edge is cut and 0 otherwise -- checked directly across all four cases. Sum this over every edge, and minimize the negative of that sum, to get the full Max-Cut QUBO.

Take a 4-node cycle: nodes 0 through 3, edges connecting each neighbor around the ring. The alternating assignment, x equals 1, 0, 1, 0, cuts all 4 edges -- the global optimum, confirmed by direct per-edge evaluation. Grouping two neighbors together instead, x equals 1, 1, 0, 0, cuts only 2 of the 4 edges. The reason the alternating pick works perfectly is that a 4-cycle is bipartite: its nodes split cleanly into two sets with no edges inside either set.

Applying the spin substitution from Lesson 3 to the per-edge term produces the standard Max-Cut cost Hamiltonian used throughout the QAOA literature: C of x equals the sum over edges of one-half times 1 minus s_i s_j. Checking this on the same two assignments, computed directly: the alternating pick gives C equals 4, and the grouped pick gives C equals 2 -- matching the QUBO totals exactly. This is the exact cost Hamiltonian QAOA's circuit is built to extremize.

Max-Cut looks abstract, but it stands in for real problems -- fraud-ring detection in transaction networks, circuit layout on a chip -- and it's provably NP-hard, making it an honest benchmark. Next lesson's lab hands you a new graph and has you build its full Q matrix yourself, brute-force confirming the optimum rather than trusting a claim.
